extracted.intended_audience: users learning to typeset with TeX / readers of The TeXbook (typographers, authors preparing documents in plain TeX)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and grammatical rules for specifying dimensions, boxes, and glue in plain TeX; how to construct and manipulate typeset material (units, magnification, box primitives, glue behavior, and sentence/word spacing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: A physical dimension should be typed as: (1) optional-sign number unit-of-measure or (2) optional-sign digitstring . digitstring unit-of-measure. An optional sign is +, -, or nothing; a digit string consists of zero or more decimal digits. The '.' can also be a ','.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blank spaces are optional before signs, numbers, and units and optional after the whole dimension, but you should not put spaces within the digits of a number or between the letters of the unit of measure. Examples: '3 in', '-.013837in', '0.mm', '29 pc', '+ 42,1 dd', '123456789sp'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always specify a unit for zero dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a dimension is zero, you must specify a unit of measure; do not just say '0'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use '0pt', '0in', etc., because the unit is required even when the magnitude is zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Units and keywords are context-sensitive and case-insensitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Unit names and other keywords are not preceded by backslashes and may be given in uppercase or mixed case; the category codes of letters are irrelevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'pt' is a keyword only when it appears after a number in a hdimeni; 'at' is a keyword only when it appears after an external font name in a \font declaration. A complete list of TeX keywords is provided: at, bp, by, cc, cm, dd, depth, em, ex, fil, height, in, l, minus, mm, mu, pc, plus, pt, scaled, sp, spread, to, true, width. (See Appendix I for contexts.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum legal dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX will not deal with dimensions whose absolute value is 230 sp or more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In other words, the maximum legal dimension is slightly less than 16384 pt (about 18.892 feet or 5.7583 meters); keep dimensions well within that range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnification must be declared early and is global
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \magnification=hnumberi where hnumberi is 1000×the desired scale factor (e.g., 1200 for 1.2×); this instruction must be given before the first page of output is completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot apply two different magnifications to the same document. Magnification affects how explicit (non-true) dimensions are interpreted in the final output (e.g., \magnification=2000 makes \vskip.5cm produce 1.0 cm in the final document).

rubrics_metrics.name: The \mag primitive and its constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: \mag is an integer parameter governing magnification that should be positive and at most 32768; its value is examined in specific cases and must not change once first examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The value of \mag is examined (1) just before the first page is shipped to the dvi file, (2) when computing a true dimension, and (3) when the dvi file is being closed (some implementations also examine it when shipping each page); because a document has only one magnification, \mag must remain constant after it has been first examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'true' units to cancel magnification
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting 'true' just before a unit (e.g., 'truept', 'truecm') causes the unit to be unmagniﬁed so magnification cancels out for that quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, after \magnification=2000, '\vskip.5truecm' is equivalent to '\vskip.25cm'. Plain TeX commonly uses 'true' in assignments like '\hsize = 6.5 true in' after a new magnification so the final printed width is as intended regardless of magnification.

rubrics_metrics.name: em and ex are relative units
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX recognizes em as the width of a 'quad' in the current font and ex as the 'x-height' of the current font; these values depend on the font.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different fonts define different em and ex values (e.g., cmr10 has 1 em = 10pt and 1 ex ≈ 4.3pt). It is generally best to use em for horizontal measurements and ex for vertical measurements that depend on the current font.

rubrics_metrics.name: hdimeni may reference registers and expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: A hdimeni can refer to TeX's internal registers or parameters, such as '\hsize', numeric multiplications like '2\wd3', fractional expressions like '.5\hsize', and negations like '-\dimen100'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete definition is given in a later chapter; for now, you may use such expressions when specifying dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box model: boxes have width, height, depth and a reference point
rubrics_metrics.description: In TeX each character or construct is a rectangular box with three associated measurements (height, width, depth) and a reference point (reference point at left edge and baseline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters' shapes may protrude outside box boundaries; baselines of adjacent characters line up because TeX aligns boxes by their reference points. Example measurements (cmr10) are given to illustrate typical values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italic correction and use of \/ when switching fonts
rubrics_metrics.description: Fonts supply an italic-correction value for characters indicating how far they extend to the right of their box; this correction is added when you type '\/' just after the character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember to use '\/' when shifting from a slanted font to an unslanted one in cases where no space intervenes, so spacing remains appropriate (example: '{\sl italic correction\/}').

rubrics_metrics.name: Black boxes, rules: \hrule and \vrule
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'black box' is a filled rectangle created with rules; horizontal rules are created with \hrule and vertical rules with \vrule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may specify any height, width, and depth, but avoid excessive black area because printers prefer white space; skinny rule boxes are used for horizontal/vertical lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: hbox and vbox primitives; composing with boxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \hbox{...} to create a horizontal box (line) and \vbox{...} to create a vertical box; TeX composes pages by pasting boxes together horizontally and vertically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You only need to use explicit hbox/vbox when you want complete control over placement (e.g., centering a heading); normal text composition is automatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative dimensions and shadow boxes are allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: A box's height, width, or depth may be negative (a 'shadow box'); TeX accepts negative dimensions and does arithmetic normally, e.g., a character's width can be negative to act like a backspace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative widths can be used to simulate some right-to-left behavior, but TeX's line-breaking algorithm assumes words don't have negative widths, so there are limits to this technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjusting boxes: \kern, \lower, \raise, and \setbox
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX can insert kerns (explicit spacing), lower or raise boxes relative to baseline, and store boxes into box registers with \setbox.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '\setbox0=\hbox{T\kern-.1667em\lower.5ex\hbox{E}\kern-.125em X}' builds the TeX logo; use these primitives to craft precise positioning inside boxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic box display with \showbox
rubrics_metrics.description: Use '\showbox<n>' after setting a box register to have TeX write a diagnostic representation of the box contents to the log file (height, depth, width, nested items).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This display format is primarily for diagnostics to understand TeX's internal box-and-glue representation when debugging complex constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glue has three attributes: natural, stretch, and shrink
rubrics_metrics.description: Glue between boxes is characterized by its natural space, its ability to stretch, and its ability to shrink; these determine how TeX sets glue when creating boxes of a specified width.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a line must be made wider, TeX proportionally distributes extra space according to the relative stretchabilities present; when narrower, it proportionally reduces glue according to shrinkabilities, but never below each glue's stated shrink limit. Once glue is set for a box it becomes rigid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines for choosing glue values
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Natural glue space should be the amount that looks best; (b) glue stretch should be the maximum extra spacing acceptable before layout looks bad; (c) glue shrink should be the maximum reduction acceptable before layout looks bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers typically specify glue values for a book layout so typists can use named skips (\smallskip, \medskip, \bigskip) rather than raw point values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predefined vertical skips: \smallskip, \medskip, \bigskip
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX defines convenient named vertical glues: \smallskip, \medskip, and \bigskip for common inter-paragraph spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, \smallskip is 3pt plus 1pt minus 1pt; use the named skips so spacing semantics can be changed centrally rather than scattering point values through the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glue specification syntax for \hskip / \vskip
rubrics_metrics.description: Horizontal glue is created with \hskip and vertical glue with \vskip; a glue specification is 'hdimeni plus hdimeni minus hdimeni' where plus/minus parts are optional and natural-space must always be given as an explicit hdimeni (even 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use constructs like '\vskip6pt plus2pt minus2pt' (plain TeX's \medskip). When using \hskip with fractional em units, follow with '\relax' if the following text could be 'plus' or 'minus' (e.g., '\hskip.5em\relax').

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite glue units (fil, fill, filll) and their orders
rubrics_metrics.description: To specify inﬁnite stretchability use 'fil', 'fill', or 'filll' units (fil is first order, fill second, filll third); e.g., \vfil is equivalent to '\vskip 0pt plus 1fil'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different orders compare as much larger inﬁnities so prefer fil where possible, use fill when you need a stronger infinity, and avoid filll unless absolutely necessary. TeX uses integer arithmetic on scaled fil units so extremely small fractional multiples may be indistinguishable from 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of infinite glue for alignment and filling
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting infinite glue at one or both ends of a horizontal list yields flush-right (left glue), centered (both ends), or other alignment effects; \vfill fills remaining vertical space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples using \line: '\line{This text will be flush left.\hfil}' or '\line{\hfil This text will be flush right.}' or '\line{\hfil This text will be centered.\hfil}'. Use \hfill, \hfil, \vfill, \vfil and their negations to control distribution of space.

rubrics_metrics.name: TeX's sophisticated sentence spacing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX inserts extra space at the end of a sentence and automatically increases stretchability (and decreases shrinkability) of the inter-sentence glue compared with inter-word glue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concretely, glue after a comma stretches at 1.25× the rate of ordinary inter-word glue; glue after a period/exclamation/question mark stretches at 3× the rate. For shrinking, comma glue shrinks to 80% of ordinary inter-word glue, and period/exclamation/question glue shrinks to 1/3. This produces nicer spacing but means TeX's sentence-end detection must be handled carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis and spaced dots: use \ldots in math mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Typing three periods in a row produces '...' with dots too close together; to get spaced ellipsis use '\ldots' in math mode (e.g., '$\ldots$').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Math formulas are exempt from normal text spacing rules, so '$\ldots$' yields ' . . . ' appropriate for an ellipsis. Chapter 18 covers \ldots and related matters in more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations and preventing sentence-end spacing: use tie (~) or control space
rubrics_metrics.description: A period after an abbreviation (Mr., Mrs., Dr., etc.) does not always indicate end-of-sentence; use a 'tie' (~) to insert a nonbreakable normal space (e.g., 'Mr.~Drofnats') or a control space '\ ' (e.g., 'Mr.\ Drofnats') to get a normal space without allowing a line break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using '~' also tells TeX not to break the line at that space; '\ ' inserts an ordinary (breakable) space but prevents TeX from treating the period as sentence-ending in some contexts.
